item.title: Meta, US states agree $16.7b settlement in landmark teen safety case
item.description:
Meta agreed to pay a coalition of US states as much as $16.7 billion and to impose sweeping new limits on how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram, according to a court filing on Wednesday that ends a landmark trial in California.

The proposed settlement, filed in federal court, would resolve claims by 29 states that Meta deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users, misled the public about the risks and unlawfully collected data from children under 13.

The changes to how young people use its apps go further than anything Meta has accepted before, and follow years of criticism from parents and experts over the effects of the world's biggest social media platforms on children.

Anger over the impact of Instagram and Facebook -- as well as rival apps like Snapchat and TikTok -- has driven the spread of age limits and school phone bans around the world.

In the United States, Meta still faces thousands of personal injury claims and litigation from school districts, none of which the agreement covers.
The case by the 29 states was among the most far-reaching, with Meta warning that a courtroom loss could have exposed it to more than $1 trillion in penalties.

"Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms -- and will do it within months," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement.

He called the outcome "real change, real transparency, and real enforceable protections for children."

The filing states that the agreement does not amount to an admission of liability or wrongdoing by Meta, which has consistently denied the allegations. It requires court approval to take effect.

The most far-reaching provisions are not financial. Meta has agreed to a long list of new safeguards that will substantially change how the apps work for young people.

One change is an automatic nighttime block that locks teenagers out of Facebook and Instagram between midnight and 6:00 am local time.

Teenage accounts will also be capped by default at two hours of cumulative daily use across Meta''s apps, though time spent messaging or watching long-form video does not count toward the limit.

Both restrictions tighten if the rest of the industry follows suit.

''Right away''

Meta framed the deal as a template for the rest of the industry and pressed its competitors to match it.

"Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution," said C.J. Mahoney, Meta''s chief legal officer.

"We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away."

Should competing platforms adopt equivalent commitments, the overnight lockout would widen to 10 pm to 7 am and the daily allowance would fall to 60 minutes per app, capped at two hours in total.

Compliance would be policed for 10 years by an independent auditor chosen jointly by Meta and the states, and paid for by the company.

The settlement payment schedule provides for 10 annual installments. California, the largest recipient, is due $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion over the decade, followed by New York with up to $1.13 billion.

The settlement ends the trial in its second week.

Instagram boss Adam Mosseri took the stand on Tuesday and admitted he touted newly launched safety tools for teens without disclosing low adoption rates from early testing several years ago.

Other witnesses testified over the past week that Meta knew the tools were not effective and even that they were "designed to fail."

Meta founder and chief executive Mark Zuckerberg had been expected to testify as well.

item.title: The foreign tourists missing in Nepal's flash floods
item.description:
NEPAL-WEATHER-FLOOD

Hundreds of tourists in Nepal, many of them foreigners, have gone missing in the Himalayan nation's devastating flash floods on Wednesday, which have killed at least 95 people.

Hours after the disaster tore through the border region with Tibet, some 403 visitors, including 341 foreign nationals, were still unaccounted for, according to the ministry of culture, tourism and civil aviation.

In its second situation update posted on X, the Nepal Tourism Board gave a tally of 384 missing travellers, 291 of them non-Nepalis. Many of the foreign tourists' nationalities were yet to be confirmed.

Nestled in the Himalayas, Nepal is a milestone tourist destination for hikers and climbers from around the world, lured by the challenge of scaling some of the world''s highest peaks, Mount Everest among them.

Here is the latest info on the missing:

India

According to the tourism board, 142 nationals from neighbouring India were missing.

The missing Indians were in the country with three travel agencies: Samrat Tours & Travels, Leaf Holiday and Himalayan Glacier.

Malaysia

Seventeen Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours & Travels were missing in the floods, the board said.

Malaysia's foreign ministry however said its embassy in Kathmandu has received reports from travel agencies suggesting they had lost contact with 11 Malaysian nationals believed to be in the Rasuwa district.

United Kingdom

Twelve UK citizens with the Alpine Eco Trek agency were unaccounted for, the tourism board said.

South Korea
South Korea officials confirmed eight hydropower workers were out of contact in the Rasuwa district following the floods.

South Africa

Four South Africans travelling with the same Alpine Eco Trek agency as the missing British citizens were missing, according to the tourism board.

United States

Three US citizens, also with Fishtail Tours & Travels, were unaccounted for, the board said.

Portugal

A Portuguese woman was missing in the floods, the foreign ministry told AFP.

"She was with a group at the border post on the Nepali side," a ministry spokeswoman said.

Australia

One Australian with Kathmandu Holiday Tours & Travel was missing, according to the board.

Netherlands

A Dutch citizen travelling with the same company as the missing Australian was also unaccounted for, the board added.

Italy

The Italian foreign ministry said two Italian tourists and their guide were stranded upstream from a landslide but are receiving assistance.

The ministry is aware of 90 Italian citizens currently in Nepal and Tibet, but does not know if any might have been affected.

Nationalities unconfirmed

Several of the tour groups also announced missing foreigners whose nationalities had not been confirmed.

They included 77 with Trekkers Society, 26 with Kailash Journey and eight with Richa Tours & Travels.

Nepal

The Nepali tourism board also announced that, in addition to the unaccounted-for foreigners, a total of 93 Nepalis were missing.

item.title: Chandpur jeweler, family missing amid allegations of unreturned pledged gold
item.description:
A Chandpur jeweler and his family have gone missing amid allegations that he failed to return gold jewelry pledged by several customers.
Pintu Das, owner of SK Shilpalay on the ground floor of Akhand Market in Chandpur city, his wife Rimi Das, and their two sons, Class 10 students Priyam Das and Rupam Das, have reportedly been untraceable since August 20, according to relatives.
The disappearance has raised concern among people who had pledged gold with Pintu, with some alleging that he went into hiding with the jewelry.
Police, however, said they are yet to establish whether Pintu and his family are missing or have gone into hiding. They are trying to locate the family.
On Wednesday, Upoma De, a close relative of Pintu and a resident of Guakhola Road in Chandpur city, informed local journalists about the matter.
“Pintu Das lived with his family in a rented house in Chandpur city. He was in debt for various reasons. We are receiving allegations that many people had pledged gold with him. We have not been able to find Pintu and his family since August 20,” she said.
Several local residents said Pintu was involved in the business of taking gold as collateral and that gold belonging to different people was pledged with him.
They said he had been unable to return the pledged gold within the agreed time. He had also borrowed money from several associations, they said.
Russell Khan, son of Mansur Khan of Raghunathpur in Chandpur Sadar upazila, said he had pledged around 2.5 bhori of gold jewelry with Pintu for Tk50,000.
“On August 19, I went to return the Tk50,000 and collect my jewelry. Pintu asked me to come the following day. When I went there, I found his shop locked. I later went to his house and found that locked too,” Russell said.
“Later, I heard from local people that Pintu had gone into hiding with his family. I filed a written complaint with Chandpur Sadar Model Police Station on Wednesday,” he added.
Zahidul Islam, a resident of South Gunrajdi in Chandpur city, said he had pledged 12 ana of gold with Pintu, while Shubhankar Majumder said he had pledged 10 ana.
They also expressed concern about recovering their pledged gold.
According to local residents, Pintu had changed business locations several times before setting up SK Shilpalay on the ground floor of Akhand Market on Comilla Road.
They alleged that he took gold from local residents as collateral in exchange for relatively small amounts of money.
Two traders in the market said Pintu rented the shop and started his business around five to six months ago. His ancestral home is in Fatikchhari upazila of Chittagong.
Pintu and his family’s sudden disappearance has sparked discussions in the area, with some residents claiming that they went into hiding.
Chandpur Sadar Model Police Station Sub-Inspector Ferdous said no one from Pintu’s family had filed a general diary regarding their disappearance.
“If Pintu Das is hiding with his family, it will be difficult to locate him. No one from his family has filed a GD either,” he said.
Officer-in-Charge Foyez Ahmed said police learned about the disappearance on Wednesday.
“I learned today that Pintu Das and three members of his family cannot be found. I have also learned that people are owed money by him and that many had pledged gold jewelry with him,” he said.
“Whether he went into hiding because of this or whether something else happened is being investigated. We are trying to locate them,” the OC added.

item.title: DSCC suspends parking fee collection at Babubazar Bridge
item.description:
The Property Department of Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) has suspended, until further orders, the ongoing lease and khas collection of parking fees at the newly constructed car parking area under Babubazar Bridge in Ward No-32.
The suspension covers 28,051.12 square feet of open space divided into four blocks, A to D.
The decision followed a report published in Jugantar on Tuesday under the headline “Public extortion using City Corporation tokens in Babubazar,” which, according to an office order, tarnished the city corporation's image.
The office order said no parking fee can be collected at the site in violation of the suspension.
It warned that legal action would be taken if anyone collects parking fees there despite the order.
Wishing to remain anonymous, a senior officer of the DMP's traffic department said the parking area will play a vital role in easing traffic congestion there.

item.title: 7 held for posing as fake CID members in Magura kidnapping attempt
item.description:
Police have detained seven members of an alleged gang for posing as members of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and attempting to kidnap a woman in Sreepur upazila of Magura.
A toy pistol, four jackets bearing the word “CID”, three helmets, a Noah microbus and eight mobile phones were recovered from their possession, police said.
Magura Superintendent of Police Molla Azad Hossain disclosed the information at a press briefing at the district police office on Wednesday.
The detainees are Asma Khatun, Md Hasanuzzaman Hasan, Md Osman Gani, Salman Shah, Md Habibur Rahman, Md Sabik, and Md Al Amin Hossain.
Police said the suspects are from Magura, Jhenaidah, Kushtia, Kurigram and other parts of the country.
According to police, a Noah microbus was moving suspiciously in the Nakol Paschimpara area of Sreepur on Tuesday night as the gang allegedly planned to kidnap a woman.
After receiving the information, police conducted an operation and reached the area at around 1:10am on Tuesday.
Police said an investigation is underway into the suspects' possible involvement in the incident based on information obtained from them.
A case has been filed with Sreepur Police Station.
SP Molla Azad Hossain said the district police was working to ensure public safety, protect human rights and curb crime.
He urged members of the public to immediately inform police about any information related to criminal activities.

item.title: Goods to go to Myanmar, payment to come from a third country
item.description:
A new opportunity has emerged for Bangladesh to export goods to war-torn Myanmar. However, because of security risks stemming from the conflict and a shortage of US dollars, businesses in Myanmar are unable to make direct payments.

They therefore want to pay for Bangladeshi goods from a third country. Meanwhile, a Bangladeshi company has applied to the National Board of Revenue (NBR) for permission to receive payment from a third country for goods exported to Myanmar. Officials concerned at the NBR told Prothom Alo that the application would be approved.

The company, A One Fish and Marine Food, applied to the NBR in July for permission to receive export proceeds from a third country. In its application, the company said Myanmar businesses were interested in importing cement, potatoes and medicines from Bangladesh.

However, due to security risks amid the conflict and a shortage of US dollars, they were unable to make direct payments. They therefore wanted to make payments for Bangladeshi goods from Singapore, Thailand or Dubai.

Bangladeshi goods are exported to Myanmar through the Teknaf land port.

Bangladeshi traders say many bridges in Myanmar have been damaged by the conflict, while road communications have also become unsafe. Demand for Bangladeshi goods has increased in areas near the border.

Asked about the matter, A One Fish and Marine Food owner MD Alam told Prothom Alo that Myanmar had few cement factories, creating strong demand for cement there.

However, obtaining the necessary no-objection certificates (NOCs) and approvals takes a long time, preventing exporters from fully capitalising on the opportunity. He added that there was also considerable potential for exporting locally produced potatoes and various energy drinks.

How the approval will work

Officials concerned at the NBR said they initially reviewed A One Fish and Marine Food’s application to receive export proceeds from a third country. They then held discussions with the banking sector. As the main objective is to facilitate exports, a decision has been made to approve the application, which will be communicated shortly.

A relevant official, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said there was no restriction from Bangladesh Bank on receiving export proceeds from a third country. The application was therefore being approved to facilitate the inflow of foreign currency.

A Bangladesh Bank circular also provides for such an arrangement. A circular issued by its Foreign Exchange Policy Department in 2018 allowed export payments to be made from a country other than the country to which the goods were exported.

However, as of Sunday, the approval had not yet reached the Teknaf Customs Station. As a result, A One Fish and Marine Food owner MD Alam is waiting to begin the exports.

“Even for such an opportunity to earn foreign currency, we have to keep going from office to office and wait,” he said.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh’s exports to Myanmar are growing. According to Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data, Bangladesh exported goods worth USD 38.9 million to Myanmar in the latest 2025–26 fiscal year, up from USD 34.8 million in 2024–25. Export items included cement and potatoes, as well as yarn and jute products.

Business has declined, but new hopes emerge

More than 100 traders are involved in the export and import of goods with Myanmar. They see new opportunities arising from the proposed economic corridor linking China with Chattogram through Myanmar. Their interest in expanding trade has also grown after China proposed establishing the corridor during the Bangladesh prime minister’s recent visit and discussions were held on Rohingya repatriation.

SM Nurul Hoque, former president of the Bangladesh–Myanmar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told Prothom Alo that trade between the two countries had fallen to around 25 per cent of its previous level following the influx of Rohingya refugees.

“Once the Rohingya issue is resolved, trade will regain momentum. If the new corridor is established, goods could be exchanged directly with China, Thailand and Vietnam as well. Lead time could fall from 10 days to one day,” he said.

On receiving payment from another country after sending goods to Myanmar, Nurul Hoque said many wealthy Myanmar businesspeople were based in Thailand and Singapore. They could therefore make payments from those countries. Such arrangements were permissible under international rules.

The conflict has caused not only a shortage of dollars in Myanmar but also weakened its banking system. Sonali Bank previously had a branch there, but that branch no longer operates. Bangladeshi medicines are also quite popular in the Myanmar market.

Abu Murshed, former president of the Cox’s Bazar Chamber of Commerce, said there were some restrictions on cement exports because of the conflict. There are concerns that the Arakan Army could use the cement to build bunkers, he said.

item.title: India recovers 7 bodies swept downstream after Nepal floods
item.description:
NEPAL-FLOODS/CHINA

Indian authorities recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be victims of devastating floods, officials said Friday, underscoring the scale of the deadly disaster.

The bodies were found floating in rivers in the Maharajganj and Kushinagar districts of Uttar Pradesh state, which borders Nepal’s southern flood-hit Chitwan region.

“Four unidentified bodies were recovered in the district on Thursday,” Maharajganj district magistrate Gaurav Singh Sogarwal told AFP.

“We think they have been swept into India from Nepal following flash floods there.”

Three more bodies were recovered in Kushinagar district, around 70 kilometres (43 miles) downstream from the frontier, a police official confirmed.

Authorities are working to identify the bodies.

At least 472 people were killed in the floods, including 469 bodies recovered in Nepal, and three in China. At least 1,400 others are missing. The seven bodies in India are not included in that toll.

item.title: I have no idea whether my three relatives are alive or dead: Nepali student in Bangladesh
item.description:
Three relatives of Tara Thapa Magar had travelled to work in one of the affected districts before the disaster struck Nepal. There has been no news of them since the flash floods. Their phones are switched off and they cannot be contacted. No one in the family knows where they are or how they are.

Sitting in Chattogram, Tara is spending every moment in anxiety. She said, “I have no idea whether my three relatives are alive or dead. I am sitting here, far from my country, simply waiting. What could be more helpless than this?”

Twenty-year-old Tara is a final-year student in the Department of Public Health at the Asian University for Women in Chattogram. Her home is in Khanda Devi Municipality of Ramechhap district, Nepal. She spoke to Prothom Alo on Thursday evening. Tara said, “I am terrified and worried. I never imagined anything this horrific could happen.”

Nepal flood death toll rises to 469: Police

Flash floods and landslides caused heavy loss of life in Nepal on Wednesday. According to the latest reports from local media, the death toll in Nepal has risen to 469. Around 1,400 people are still missing across Nepal and Tibet. A large number of them are foreign tourists and pilgrims travelling to Kailash-Manasarovar.

Preliminary assessments suggest that a large mass of ice, rocks and earth near the Tibetan border fell into a river, triggering a powerful surge of mud and rocks through the Bhotekoshi basin. The surge flowed downstream through the Trishuli River, causing extensive damage to settlements, roads, bridges and power infrastructure. Rescue operations are still under way in remote areas. The floods have directly affected three districts.

The authorities at the Asian University for Women said 40 students from Nepal are studying at the university. Since the disaster, they have been trying to contact their families. Some are sharing verified information and emergency contact numbers, while others are organising efforts to collect aid for people affected by the disaster.

Tara Thapa Magar, Nepali student studying in BangladeshAt first, I was very frightened. I could not reach my relatives by phone. No one could say where they were or what had happened to them.

Tara first learnt about the floods on Facebook. As soon as she saw the news, she tried to contact her family members and relatives. She managed to speak to close family members living in the city, who are safe. However, she could not contact her relatives in the village because of internet connectivity problems.

The area where Tara’s family lives is also safe so far. There have been no reports of major damage. However, communications have broken down in the district where her three missing relatives were working. Disruptions to phone networks and road links have made it difficult to obtain reliable information.

Referring to these circumstances, Tara told Prothom Alo, “At first, I was very frightened. I could not reach my relatives by phone. No one could say where they were or what had happened to them. Apart from my three relatives, the other members of my family are safe.”

Tara is also worried that flooding could begin in her own area. But her greatest concern now is for her three missing relatives. She said, “Like my family, many families are waiting for news of their missing loved ones. The most urgent task now is to find them.”

Friend’s uncle missing

Sushmita Roka, a resident of Tanahun, Nepal, is also a final-year student in the Public Health Department at Asian University for Women. Her parents are safe in Kathmandu, and their home in Tanahun has not suffered any major damage. However, people she knows have been affected by the disaster.

One of Sushmita’s neighbours, an army officer, was caught in the floods. The uncle of a close friend of hers had been working in Rasuwa. He has been unreachable since the disaster.

Sushmita told Prothom Alo, “I called home as soon as I heard the news. I felt somewhat relieved after learning that my parents were safe. But someone I know is still missing. It is painful to think about what his family must be going through.”

Sushmita received news of the floods through the media and social media within an hour of the incident. Since then, she has been regularly checking on her family and acquaintances.

She said she had learnt that bodies swept downstream from the affected areas were also being recovered from the Trishuli River in Tanahun. This has spread panic among people living along the river. She also learnt that identifying the rescued bodies has become a major challenge.

Sushmita said, “Some are searching for their relatives, while others are waiting for a phone call. Bodies are being found in some places, but their identities remain unknown. Families at least want to know where their loved ones are.”

Nepali students in Bangladesh are now trying to support one another. Sushmita said the Women Nepali Students’ Organisation Bangladesh, in coordination with the Nepal Embassy, is sharing the official online donation address of the Nepal government. They are also appealing for support for rescue, relief, medical treatment, shelter and rehabilitation.

Sushmita said, “We cannot go to Nepal and stand beside the people there. But we are trying to ensure that accurate information and appeals for assistance reach people.”

‘A terrible incident’

No one in Anita Timalsina’s family, who are from Lalitpur, Nepal, has been directly affected. Their home is far from the flood-hit areas. However, images and videos of the devastation circulating on social media have left her deeply distressed.

Anita, 22, is a third-year Public Health student. She said, “My mind is in Nepal. I cannot concentrate on anything. Images and videos of the floods keep flashing before my eyes. Sitting so far away, I feel completely helpless.”

Anita first saw news of the floods on Facebook. She then contacted her family and learnt that everyone was safe. However, the scale of the disaster has left them shocked as well.

Anita said, “I saw pictures and videos of the floods on Facebook. It is a terrible incident. No one could have imagined such a disaster. So many people have lost their homes, land, families and livelihoods. Sitting far away, I am only trying to imagine what they must be going through.”

The three students believe that, alongside rescue operations, shelter, food, clean water, clothing and medicines are among the most urgent needs in the affected areas. They have called for missing people to be found quickly and for rescuers to reach those who remain stranded.

Anita said, “In such difficult times, even a small act of support can mean a great deal to someone. I hope Bangladesh and the international community will stand beside the people affected in Nepal.”

item.title: Fresh flood warnings for disaster-hit Nepal and Tibet, 1,400 still missing
item.description:
TOPSHOT-NEPAL-WEATHER-LANDSLIDE-FLOODS

China and Nepal warned of fresh flooding risks, complicating rescuers’ search Friday for more than 1,400 people missing after a deadly deluge and landslides swept away entire villages along their remote Himalayan border.

Emergency teams have recovered 392 bodies after a devastating tsunami-like wall of freezing water and mud wiped out towns under a torrent of sludge, burying homes, smashing bridges and dams and sweeping away vehicles.

Many of the missing are foreign tourists, including trekkers in the Himalayan nation and scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.

The US Geological Survey (USGS) said the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris.

Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.

Emergency teams were racing to pluck survivors from affected zones, while Nepali soldiers used sniffer dogs to search for bodies buried under the suffocating dirt.

But their efforts are hampered by fears of new floods as water trapped by the immense piles of debris blocking the valley risks surging out.

Chinese authorities warned that a lake formed by the Wednesday’s mudslide faces a “high risk of breaching and sending floodwaters downstream”, according to state media late Thursday.

Kathmandu’s Flood Forecasting Division separately issued a “special notice”, warning of a growing lake behind debris left by the landslide and urging extreme caution.

Thousands still missing

Survivors in a makeshift Nepali hospital endured an agonising wait for news of their missing loved ones.

Kula Priya said she had lost everything when the deluge hit—including her eldest son, who is missing.

“I don’t care for wealth. I just want my son back. If any of you could rescue my son, please do it for me,” she said.

“I don’t know where to go. We had three houses, all of which were washed away by the floods.”

Nepali police say they had recovered 389 bodies.

A further 910 people, including 517 foreign tourists, are out of contact in the country.

Beijing said 100 Chinese citizens—not accounted for in that tally—are also missing in Nepal.

Indians make up the largest number of missing foreigners, while the United States said 90 of its citizens were out of contact.

Across the border in Tibet—where the only sources of information are Chinese authorities—officials say hundreds are missing and three have died.

Chinese authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists—as well as 499 local residents—from Tibet.

Authorities have mobilised nearly 800 emergency workers, as well as sniffer dogs, speed boats, satellites and drones to help the rescue efforts, the state-run Xinhua new agency said.

‘Inland tsunami’

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who urged the nation to “stand together” hours after the disaster, toured some of the hardest-hit areas on Thursday.

Shah told local authorities to “provide immediate relief to displaced families” and to open blocked roads, his office said in a statement.

Other foreigners out of contact include citizens from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa and South Korea, Nepal’s tourism board said.

The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami”, travelling nearly 170 kilometres (105 miles) south into Nepal, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble, of Australia’s La Trobe University.

Buddhist spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, who lives in exile in India, said he would “pray for all those who have lost their lives”.

Glacial collapse

The USGS said a glacial collapse caused seismic activity and had “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.

“This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake,” it said, but the seismic recordings were analysed and it was found instead to be a “glacial collapse and debris flow”.

Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among the hundreds missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, on the Chinese side of the border.

Logadarrsiny Raman, 26, from Malaysia, said her parents, aunt and uncle were on a pilgrimage but she lost contact with them after dawn on Wednesday.

Raman said the travel agency told her its last contact with the group of 17 Malaysians was at 8:18 am Nepal time, when they were travelling towards the Nepal-China border.

The flood crashed into the area where they last were soon after.

“I’m very anxious,” she told AFP. “My only hope is to hear back from them that they are safe.”

item.title: 2,578 Bangladeshis seek asylum in UK in 2026
item.description:
A total of 2,578 people from Bangladesh claimed asylum in the United Kingdom in the first half of 2026, including 1,483 in the first quarter and 1,095 in the second quarter, according to the lasted data released by UK Home Office.

Of the 2,578 people, 1,649 were main applicants and 929 were dependants. Main applicants accounted for about 64 per cent of the total, while dependants made up the remaining 36 per cent.

There were 946 main applicants and 537 dependants in Q1, compared with 703 main applicants and 392 dependants in Q2. The number of main applicants therefore fell by 243, or 25.7 per cent, while dependants declined by 145, or 27 per cent.

The Home Office defines an asylum claim as an individual’s entry into the UK asylum system. A claim can cover more than one person when family members are included as dependants. Its dataset counts both main applicants and dependants when measuring the number of people claiming asylum.

UK asylum applications drop by more than a fifth

Nearly 77pc aged 18 to 49

People aged 18 to 29 formed the largest age group, with 1,144 people, or 44.4 per cent of the total. This was followed by those aged 30 to 49, with 831, or 32.2 per cent.

Together, the two groups accounted for 1,975 people, or 76.6 per cent of all Bangladeshi people claiming asylum in the first six months of the year.

The number of people aged 18 to 29 fell from 659 in Q1 to 485 in Q2, a decline of 174, or 26.4 per cent. Those aged 30 to 49 fell from 473 to 358, down 115, or 24.3 per cent.

People aged 17 or under accounted for 554, or about 21.5 per cent, of the total. Their number fell from 322 in Q1 to 232 in Q2, a decline of 90, or 28 per cent.

There were 38 people aged 50 to 69 and 11 aged 70 or over during the period. The 50–69 age group fell from 23 in Q1 to 15 in Q2, while those aged 70 and over declined from six to five.

Men made up nearly 60pc

Men accounted for 1,527, or about 59.2 per cent, of the 2,578 people claiming asylum, compared with 1,051 women, or 40.8 per cent.

In Q1, there were 894 males and 589 females. The numbers fell to 633 males and 462 females in Q2.

The decline was therefore much sharper among men, whose number fell by 261, or 29.2 per cent, compared with a fall of 127, or 21.6 per cent, among women.

Most were dependants among under-18s

The age breakdown also shows a sharp difference between main applicants and dependants among younger claimants.

Of the 554 people aged 17 or under, only four were main applicants across the two quarters, while 550 were dependants.

In Q1, the under-18 group comprised 320 dependants and two main applicants. In Q2, there were 230 dependants and two main applicants.

By contrast, among people aged 18 to 29, there were 954 main applicants and 190 dependants across the two quarters. Among those aged 30 to 49, 650 were main applicants and 181 were dependants.

Almost all claims made inside UK

Most Bangladeshi people claiming asylum did so inside the UK rather than at a port.

Of the 2,578 people recorded in the first half, 2,554 claimed in the country, while 24 were recorded as claiming at a UK port.

Q1 accounted for 18 port claims and 1,465 in-country claims. In Q2, the figures were six and 1,089, respectively.

One UASC recorded in Q2

Almost all Bangladeshi claimants were classified as non-UASC, meaning they were not unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC).

The Q1 data recorded no UASC, while Q2 recorded one UASC, a male main applicant aged 17 or under who made his claim in the country.

The Home Office describes UASCs as children who arrive in the UK without a parent or legal guardian to care for them. In the wider UK asylum system, UASCs accounted for 5 per cent of people claiming asylum in the year ending June 2026.

Bangladesh was also among the six nationalities with the largest numbers of people claiming asylum in the UK in the year ending June 2026, according to the Home Office. The six nationalities—Pakistan, Eritrea, Iran, Sudan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh—together accounted for 46 per cent of people claiming asylum during that period.

item.description:
Rescue teams waded through mud on Thursday searching for more than 1,400 people missing after flash floods and landslides struck the Nepal-Tibet border, as the death toll rose sharply to at least 362, with entire villages swept away.
Experts warned of the risk of further floods a day after the devastating tsunami-like wall of freezing water and mud wiped out towns under a torrent of sludge, engulfing homes, smashing bridges and dams, and sweeping vehicles away like toys.
Many of the missing are foreign tourists, including scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris.
Emergency teams were racing to pluck survivors from affected zones, while Nepali soldiers used sniffer dogs to search for bodies buried under the suffocating dirt.
“Everything is finished,” Omkar Joshi, a 35-year-old Nepali customs agent rescued from a hilltop in the border town of Timure, told AFP.
“It is a giant graveyard. All that is left are sand and pebbles, soaked red by human blood.”
Nepali police said they had recovered 359 bodies.
Another 910 people, including 517 foreign tourists, were out of contact in the country. Beijing said 100 Chinese citizens are missing in Nepal.
In China, state media said the “mudslide disaster” at the Gyirong Port in Tibet killed three people, while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, are missing.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the area on Thursday, state media said, to oversee “emergency rescue and relief work, and to visit rescue workers and affected people”.
Li Qipu, a member of China’s paramilitary People’s Armed Police, cited “the instability of a reservoir lake upstream” and “the narrow mountain road” as elements complicating rescue efforts.
China’s Tibet Autonomous Region is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists.
‘Inland tsunami’
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who urged the Himalayan nation to “stand together” hours after the disaster, visited some of the hardest-hit areas on Thursday.
Shah told local authorities to “provide immediate relief to displaced families” and to open blocked roads, his office said in a statement.
The foreigners out of contact included Indians and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea and the United States, Nepal’s tourism board said.
The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami”, travelling nearly 170 kilometres south into Nepal, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble, of Australia’s La Trobe University.
Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected, but deaths were reported as far south as Chitwan, on the border with India.
Buddhist spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, who lives in exile in India, said he would “pray for all those who have lost their lives”.
Chinese government officials in Tibet mobilised nearly 800 emergency workers, as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, the official Xinhua news agency said.
Promises of aid and assistance came in soon after reports of the scale of the disaster.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was sending emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags.

item.title: How an avalanche unleashed Nepal catastrophe
item.description:
A massive ice-and-rock avalanche in Nepal’s high Himalayas appears to have temporarily dammed a river before the blockage collapsed, unleashing the catastrophic flood that tore through the Nepal-China border region on Wednesday, scientists say, as authorities warn the danger of further flooding has not passed.
The disaster sent a wall of water, mud and boulders down the Bhotekoshi river corridor, devastating settlements and infrastructure and leaving a heavy death toll and hundreds unaccounted for.
According to the Kathmandu Post, scientists analysing satellite imagery increasingly believe an avalanche blocked the Lhende river, creating a temporary natural dam. When that barrier gave way, the accumulated water surged downstream into the Bhotekoshi.
Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, a climate researcher and professor at Kathmandu University, told the newspaper that an avalanche on the Nepal side was suspected of blocking the Lhende.
A magnitude-4.4 earthquake was recorded in Tibet around the same time, but scientists have yet to establish whether it contributed to triggering the avalanche.
The Kathmandu Post also cited journalist Kunda Dixit of Nepali Times as reporting that an avalanche struck the northern face of the 7,245-metre Langtang Lirung, sending debris into the river system.
Scientists at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) are examining satellite imagery to establish the precise sequence of events.
Preliminary evidence indicates a huge volume of ice and rock entered the Lhende, possibly accumulating at a narrow section and forming a temporary landslide dam, according to the Kathmandu Post.
The scale of the resulting surge was extraordinary.
The newspaper, citing ICIMOD, reported that the Trishuli river rose by as much as nine metres within 30 minutes at Galchhi and about seven metres at Malekhu.
The region was already considered highly vulnerable.
A sudden Bhotekoshi flood in July last year was attributed to a glacial lake outburst near the Nepal-China border.
Research by ICIMOD and the UN Development Programme has identified 3,624 glacial lakes across Nepal, India and Tibet, 47 of them potentially dangerous.
The latest disaster has also renewed concerns over the increasing instability of the Himalayan cryosphere as temperatures rise.
“The risk is still there,” Kayastha told the Kathmandu Post, warning that warming increases the likelihood of glacier melt, ice-and-rock collapse and avalanches, although scientists cannot predict exactly where the next disaster will strike.
That warning has taken on added urgency with the formation of another large barrier lake.
This report was compiled from reporting by the Kathmandu Post and Global Times, with the latter citing Chinese government agencies and state media.

item.title: Bangladeshi among 15 killed in fire at Russia’s Amur gas complex

Another Bangladeshi worker remains missing, while seven others were seriously injured, said Mizanur Rahman, the embassy’s first secretary (labour).
The deceased was identified as Zakir Hossain, from Bhairab in Kishoreganj. The missing worker, Md Alal Hossain Raju, is from Gangni in Meherpur.
Mizanur said some bodies were badly burned and could not yet be identified. Raju may be among the unidentified remains, he said.
According to Reuters, AGCC initially reported seven deaths, including six Chinese nationals, on Wednesday. The company later raised the death toll to 15 in a post on its Telegram channel on Thursday, saying 14 of the dead were foreign nationals.
AGCC said the fire originated in an auxiliary section of a pyrolysis unit before spreading. The complex’s main equipments were not damaged, it said. Mizanur said arrangements were underway to transfer the seven seriously injured Bangladeshi workers from Amur to a specialised hospital in Moscow. Six are currently in intensive care.
The embassy has contacted the relevant authorities to arrange the repatriation of Zakir’s body. The embassy will also continue discussions with LLC Sinopec Engineering Group regarding Zakir’s outstanding dues and compensation, Mizanur said.

item.description:
A massive barrier lake formed in northern Nepal following Wednesday’s devastating floods and mudslides is already overflowing and faces a high risk of breaching within the next three days, raising fears of another destructive surge as rescuers search for hundreds of missing people.
China’s Ministry of Water Resources estimated the lake contained around 2 million cubic metres of water as of Thursday morning, while another 3 million cubic metres could flow into it over the next three days, according to China Central Television, as reported by the Global Times.
The development threatens to compound a disaster that has already devastated communities along the Nepal-China border and left hundreds missing, including large numbers of foreign nationals.
According to the Kathmandu Post, the barrier lake has formed near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers in Nepal.
Chinese authorities said the lake was already overflowing and warned that continued inflows could trigger a breach.
Chinese Ministry of Water Resources is monitoring its development and conducting flood simulations to assess how a sudden release of water could affect downstream areas and emergency operations.
The Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo originate in Tibet and merge before crossing into Nepal, where the river is known as the Bhotekoshi, a major upper tributary of the Trishuli.
A breach could unleash another sudden surge downstream, posing fresh risks to communities and infrastructure along a river system already battered by Wednesday’s disaster.
The warning comes as Nepal and China continue massive rescue operations following the catastrophic floods and mudslides along their border.
The disaster struck Nepal’s Rasuwa region on Wednesday morning before causing severe destruction around the border.
Roads, bridges, buildings and other infrastructure were swept away or damaged as floodwaters and debris surged through the area and downstream.
The Global Times reported Thursday that rescue operations were being complicated by continued rainfall, unstable terrain and the danger of secondary disasters, including the newly formed barrier lake.
Chinese authorities have mobilised emergency responders, military personnel, engineering teams and aircraft for rescue and relief operations.
Authorities on both sides of the border are still working to establish the full scale of the casualties and locate those missing.
Chinese officials said hydrological monitoring and simulations would continue as authorities prepare for the possibility of the barrier lake giving way.

item.title: Third Terminal inches closer to take-off after years of delay
item.description:
The long wait to bring Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport’s Third Terminal into operation could finally end in December, with aviation authorities completing the evaluation of a Japanese company’s proposal to run the facility and preparing to enter the crucial negotiation stage.
The Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) has completed its assessment of the company’s technical and financial proposals, clearing a major hurdle towards an operating agreement for the terminal, which has remained largely unused despite being virtually complete for years.
Negotiations are expected to begin in the first week of September, with officials aiming to sign a final agreement in October and proceed with a limited-scale soft opening on December 16, according to CAAB sources.
The development provides the clearest timeline yet for making the Tk-thousands-of-crores aviation infrastructure operational after prolonged uncertainty over who would operate and maintain it.
The Japanese company submitted its Request for Proposal (RFP) to CAAB last Tuesday. An evaluation committee subsequently assessed its technical capability before reviewing the financial proposal.
S M Lablu Rahman, CAAB member (Administration) and chairman of the proposal evaluation committee, said the evaluation process had been completed.
“As the next step, we will hold discussions with the Japanese company. After the discussions, there will be an agreement. We are moving toward our target of a soft opening by December 16,” he told Bangla Tribune.
“We hope we will be able to complete everything within the stipulated time.”
Construction of the Third Terminal began on December 30, 2019, and it was ceremonially soft-opened in October 2023 after more than 99% of the project was completed.
Yet passengers have not been able to use the facility for regular operations for nearly three years amid delays in finalising its operation and maintenance arrangements.
Air Commodore Abu Sayeed Mehboob Khan, CAAB member for Operations and Planning and vice-chairman of the evaluation committee, said the RFP followed lengthy discussions with the Japanese side.
“If everything goes well, we hope we will be able to reach a final agreement within a short time,” he said.
“If everything remains in order, it will be possible to open the terminal on December 16 as announced by the government.”
Preparations are meanwhile underway for the proposed opening, including system testing, recruitment and staff training, security arrangements and coordination among immigration, airlines, ground handlers and other agencies.
The 230,000-square-metre terminal is expected to dramatically expand the country’s main international airport.
The existing first and second terminals can handle around 8 million passengers annually; with the Third Terminal operational, total capacity is expected to rise to as many as 20 million passengers a year.
It will have parking facilities for 37 aircraft, 100 check-in counters, 10 self-check-in kiosks, 16 regular baggage belts and four dedicated belts for oversized baggage.
The terminal also includes automated baggage-handling facilities, modern baggage storage, airline lounges, baby-care facilities, children’s play areas, health inspection and first-aid rooms, disease-testing facilities and an isolation area.
For CAAB, however, the immediate challenge is no longer construction but turning the completed infrastructure into a functioning airport terminal.
If negotiations begin as scheduled in September and culminate in an agreement in October, December 16 could finally mark the beginning of passenger operations at a terminal that has spent years waiting for take-off.

item.title: David Emon’s second-in-command Mobarak held after Fatikchhari shootout
item.description:
Police arrested notorious criminal Mobarak Hossain from the false ceiling of a washroom in Fatikchhari, Chittagong, following a tense hours-long operation on early Wednesday.
Mobarak is known as the second-in-command of jailed top criminal David Emon and is allegedly involved in several killings, including the murder of Jubo Dal leader Masud in Raozan.
He opened fire at police from the false ceiling during the raid, firing six rounds and injuring five police personnel, including Chittagong Additional Superintendent of Police Kazi Md Tarek Aziz.
Police arrested him after his firearm jammed. Three of his associates, Md Raihan, Md Farid and Md Nasir, were also arrested from the house.
Acting on a tip-off, police surrounded a house in Shahnagar area of Lelang Union around 3am on Tuesday. After the occupants refused to open the iron gate, police broke it down at around 4:30am in the presence of local residents.
Officers entered the house and found Mobarak hiding in the washroom’s false ceiling. He opened fire as police approached, injuring five officers.
The injured include Additional SP Tarek Aziz, Fatikchhari Police Station OC Robiul Alam Khan, Aziz’s bodyguard Constable Mamunur Rashid, and Constables Shah Newaz and Saddam Hossain. They received medical treatment.
Tarek Aziz, who led the operation, said police had learned of Mobarak’s whereabouts after arresting David Emon on July 29. Several raids were subsequently conducted in the remote hills of Fatikchhari, but Mobarak evaded arrest.
On Monday, police arrested four of his associates, Arafat, Md Munna, Iqbal and Babul, during a raid in the Kanchannagar hills.
Police said Mobarak later left the hills and took shelter at a house belonging to an acquaintance in Shahnagar, apparently considering it safer.
Tarek Aziz said police found Mobarak’s associate Raihan hiding inside the false ceiling above a washroom after entering the house. He was arrested from there. Police later detained two other associates, Nasir and Farid, from inside the false ceiling.
“Since the criminals could open fire on police from inside, the operation team proceeded cautiously. At one point, Mobarak was found hiding in the false ceiling of a washroom inside one of the rooms. As police entered the room, he opened fire with a Brazilian-made Taurus pistol. Police returned fire.
“Mobarak fired six rounds, while police fired seven. One of the bullets passed close to Tarek Aziz’s ear. Mobarak’s pistol jammed when he attempted to fire the seventh round. Police then brought him down from the false ceiling and recovered the weapon.
“The pistol had been looted from Kotwali Police Station in Chittagong city on August 5, 2024. After Mobarak’s arrest, police conducted raids in Fatikchhari and Raozan until 10pm on Wednesday to recover more weapons.”
Tarek Aziz said police sought Mobarak’s remand in two cases—one over the looting of the firearm and another over the attack on police. On Thursday, a court granted him eight days’ remand—four days in each case.
The remand was granted in the two separate cases filed with Fatikchhari Police Station over the weapon theft and attack on police.
Superintendent of Chittagong Police Md Masud Alam said Mobarak was a notorious criminal who used remote hilly areas as safe hideouts, making it difficult for police to arrest him.
“Acting on a tip-off, police arrested Mobarak and his associates. He has admitted to involvement in several killings, including the murder of Jubo Dal leader Masud in Raozan,” he said.
Police recovered a 9mm foreign-made pistol, a 7.65mm foreign-made pistol, a foreign-made revolver and a locally made pistol, along with ammunition, three magazines and spent bullet casings.

From content creation to entrepreneurship: Anamika Akter’s journey beyond social media
item.description:
Alongside establishing her identity in the entertainment industry, Anamika Akter is gradually strengthening her position through content creation and entrepreneurship.
Online, she is widely known as Queen Girl Anamika.
From an early age, Anamika had a strong desire to present herself to the public. Over time, that interest evolved into a new journey involving content creation, music videos and entrepreneurship.
Born and raised in Bancharampur, Brahmanbaria, Anamika gradually built a presence on social media by making the most of limited opportunities and her own determination. Today, she has become known online as Queen Girl Anamika.
Alongside regularly connecting with audiences through content creation, Anamika has also appeared in several music videos. Her notable works include Tomar Jonno Bhalobasha and Hridoye Acho Tumi.
Her work on social media has not only brought her popularity but has also given her the confidence to explore new opportunities by putting her interests and creativity to work.
Anamika said: “I am currently a content creator, influencer and entrepreneur. The love and support I receive from people always inspire me to do better. I want to take on better work in the future and expand my identity on a larger scale.”
Alongside content creation, Anamika has also embarked on a journey as an entrepreneur. She runs a clothing store under the name Queen Girl Anamika, through which she also delivers clothing to customers via its online outlet.
On one hand, she is pursuing entertainment and content creation, while on the other, she is developing her own business.
For Anamika, this journey is not simply about gaining popularity; it is also an opportunity to turn her dreams into reality.
Her journey demonstrates that social media is no longer merely a platform for entertainment. When used effectively, it can create opportunities for young people to build recognition, develop careers and establish their own businesses.
Queen Girl Anamika is now moving forward along that path. While expanding her work as a content creator, music video artist and entrepreneur, she dreams of working on an even larger scale in the future.
Her goal is simple—to continue moving forward step by step with the love of her audience and her own hard work, while building a strong and lasting identity for herself.

Youth on the climate frontline: Ready to act, still barred from power
item.description:
When floodwater enters a home in Bangladesh’s haor region, climate adaptation stops being an abstract policy term. For girls and young women, it can mean protecting food and drinking water, caring for children and older relatives, and keeping a household functioning while movement outside becomes difficult or unsafe.
This reality is often missing from national and international climate debates. Young people experience climate hazards not only as floods, cyclones and extreme heat, but also as interrupted education, lost income, unsafe mobility, damaged homes and uncertainty about the future. They also do far more to protect their communities than is usually recognized.
A qualitative study commissioned by Plan International Bangladesh and conducted by Global MindLens examined youth roles in locally led climate adaptation across Bhola, Barguna, Kurigram, Sunamganj and Dhaka.
The research completed 48 focus group discussions, 78 key informant interviews and 15 observation and institutional-process reviews across coastal, haor, char and riverine, and urban settings. Across these different contexts, one pattern repeatedly emerged: young people are active in preparedness, response and recovery, but remain weakly represented when priorities, budgets and long-term adaptation decisions are set.
Before a disaster, young people spread warnings, identify local risks, help households prepare food and water, and mobilize communities. During floods, cyclones or extreme heat, they support evacuation, rescue, urgent communication and assistance to children, older people and persons with disabilities.
Girls and young women frequently sustain food, water, care and household safety — essential climate work that remains largely invisible.
Their contribution continues after the emergency through relief support, cleanup, damage reporting, home repair and recovery. Yet their influence falls sharply when decisions move into formal planning, resource allocation, service monitoring and accountability.
Institutions rely on youth action during a crisis but rarely share authority with them afterward.
That is the policy gap. Young people should not be treated only as beneficiaries, campaign audiences or emergency volunteers. They are also local risk analysts, communicators, organizers and potential accountability actors.
The real test of inclusion is not how many young people attend an activity, but whether their knowledge changes a priority, service, budget or decision.
Bangladesh’s youth-climate challenge is not a shortage of interest, courage or ideas. It is a failure of institutional design.
Young people are regularly invited to awareness sessions, volunteer activities and consultations. Yet participation often ends at the microphone.
Their proposals may not be formally recorded, assigned to a responsible authority, linked to a budget, given a response deadline or followed by feedback. Attendance is counted and activities are reported, while power and resources remain largely unchanged.
The barriers are greatest for those already facing exclusion. Girls and young women may confront restrictions related to family permission, unsafe travel, meeting times and care responsibilities.
Poorer youth bear the hidden cost of unpaid participation: a meeting can mean lost income. Youth with disabilities face inaccessible venues, transportation and communication. These disadvantages can overlap, making nominal inclusion meaningless.
Policy must therefore move from invitation to accountability. Participation should be designed, financed and monitored so that young people — especially girls, poorer youth, younger adolescents, youth with disabilities and those in informal settlements — can enter decision spaces safely and influence what happens there.
Bangladesh needs more than another broad promise to “engage youth.” Drawing on the study findings, I propose a Five-S Youth Climate Compact as a practical framework for piloting and evaluation.
It is not a finished model, but a testable approach for governments, donors and development partners seeking measurable youth influence in climate action.
Seat: Give young people transparent representation in local adaptation, disaster-risk reduction, contingency planning and service monitoring. Selection must include marginalized youth, not only those already educated, connected or visible.
Skills: Link training in early warning, first aid, risk communication, safeguarding, mapping and monitoring to defined public roles. Training should lead to responsibility, not certificates without a pathway to action.
Seed resources: Finance local solutions, not only meetings. Small grants, equipment, transportation and communication support can enable youth to test flood-warning, heat-risk mapping, accessible evacuation, drainage-monitoring and school-continuity initiatives.
Safety and accessibility: Build safe venues, suitable timing, accessible communication, transportation support and disability-inclusive arrangements into program design and budgets. These conditions determine who can participate and whose evidence reaches decision-makers.
System of response: Record every youth proposal, assign it to a named focal person, set a response deadline and provide public feedback showing what was accepted, funded, delayed or rejected — and why.
The investment logic is simple: representation without skills is symbolic; skills without resources are underused; resources without safety exclude the most vulnerable; and participation without institutional response produces frustration rather than influence.
The model can be piloted at union and ward levels, linked to existing local government and disaster-management structures, and assessed through a simple question: Did youth participation change a plan, budget, service or institutional decision?
That should become the real measure of youth engagement in climate adaptation.
A common accountability standard is necessary, but implementation must reflect local climate realities.
In coastal districts, youth roles should focus on cyclone preparedness, evacuation, shelter safety and relief monitoring. In haor areas — seasonally flooded wetland basins — the priorities are flood warning, household resilience, school continuity and recovery.
In char and riverine communities, where people live on shifting river islands and erosion-prone land, youth systems must be mobility-sensitive, disability-inclusive and connected to livelihoods and social protection.
In Dhaka, youth can map heat and waterlogging risks, monitor drainage and waste failures, identify unsafe routes and report directly to ward and City Corporation authorities.
Bangladesh’s National Adaptation Plan and Delta Plan 2100, together with the Sendai Framework and Action for Climate Empowerment, already support participation and inclusive resilience. The gap is local execution.
Donors, development partners and public institutions should therefore fund clear youth mandates, dedicated resources, named institutional responsibility and measurable feedback.
The principle is straightforward: 1 national standard for rights and accountability, 4 local missions for action and results.
Meaningful youth leadership can be measured by a simple question: when a young person reports a blocked drain, an unsafe evacuation route, an inaccessible venue or a flood-risk hotspot, can they see who is responsible, when action is due, whether resources were allocated and what changed?
When that chain is missing, participation is symbolic.
The required shift is now clear: from inviting youth to activities to embedding them in institutions; from depending on unpaid youth labor to financing youth-led solutions; and from hearing youth concerns to providing documented responses.
Bangladesh’s experience carries a wider lesson for climate-vulnerable countries: youth participation becomes meaningful only when it is connected to authority, resources and accountability.
Young people are already on the climate frontline. Institutions must now bring them into the rooms where priorities, budgets and decisions are made.

item.title: Lotus blooms turn Kalijug Beel into natural kaleidoscope
item.description:
White lotus flowers have transformed Kalijug Beel in Pirganj into a picturesque natural attraction, drawing thousands of visitors from different parts of the country.
The wetland, located in Kalijug village of Jabarhat Union, about 13 kilometres south of Pirganj upazila town of Thakurgaon, is now covered with blooming lotuses.
The sight is particularly striking in the early morning and late afternoon, when the white flowers sway gently in the breeze against the tranquil backdrop of the wetland.
Visitors start arriving early in the morning, with families, friends and groups gathering to enjoy the scenery and take photographs. A wooden footbridge is currently the only access route into the lotus-covered area.
Local residents said the naturally formed lotus wetland has become one of the area's most popular attractions. They, however, urged visitors to protect the environment and refrain from damaging or plucking the flowers.
Shahana Parvin, who came from Dinajpur while visiting relatives in Ranisankail, said she decided to visit the site after hearing about it.
“Having boats to take visitors around the beel would make the experience even better,” she said.
School student Nigar said she had heard about Kalijug Beel only a few days earlier and persuaded her parents to take her there.
“I was happy to see so many lotus flowers, but I felt bad when I saw some people plucking them,” she said.
Nafisa, who visited the beel with two friends from Bangladesh University of Professionals in Dhaka, said they were fascinated to see a lotus wetland after reading about such places in books and magazines.
She suggested developing the area in a planned manner by introducing boating facilities, restaurants, washrooms and better transport links.
“With proper planning and basic facilities, this place could attract many more tourists,” she said.
Chan Bania, a resident of Kalijug village, said visitors arrive at the beel every day from distant areas.
“Our homes are located just west of the beel. Many visitors enter our houses without permission, which makes us uncomfortable,” he said.
Pirganj Upazila Agriculture Officer Agriculturist Nazmul Hasan said lotus is an aquatic plant that spreads naturally.
“Lotus seeds can be carried by birds and fall into wetlands, from where new plants grow and gradually spread,” he said.
He added that Kalijug Porabeel is now extensively covered with lotus flowers and has emerged as a tourist attraction.
Professor Abu Bakkar Siddique, former principal of Thakurgaon Government Women's College, said lotus flowers have several medicinal properties.
He said the flower was once common in Bangladesh's wetlands but has become increasingly rare as many wetlands and water bodies have been filled or degraded.
“Steps should be taken to expand lotus growth and conserve the flower considering its importance,” he said.
Pirganj Upazila Nirbahi Officer Golam Rabbani Sardar said the naturally grown white lotuses had added a unique dimension to the area's natural beauty.
“It is truly pleasing to see people coming here from different places,” he said.
He urged visitors to enjoy the beauty without damaging the environment or plucking the flowers.
The local administration, in coordination with the union parishad, will maintain necessary monitoring to protect the area and preserve the wetland, he added.

item.title: River dredging project stalled as Sunamganj haor farmers face triple crisis
item.description:
A long-delayed river dredging project has left hundreds of thousands of Boro farmers in Sunamganj facing a triple crisis of flash floods, waterlogging and irrigation shortages.
Farmers say the failure to restore the drainage capacity of the region's rivers is delaying rice transplantation, creating irrigation problems during the dry season and increasing the risk of crop losses from early monsoon rains.
Sunamganj is one of the country's major Boro-producing districts. About 350,000 farmers cultivate Boro rice on around 223,000 hectares of land every year. In a normal season, the district produces approximately 1.15 million tonnes of paddy, equivalent to about 950,000 tonnes of rice.
Despite decades of investment in flood-protection embankments, the lack of regular river dredging has severely disrupted the natural drainage system of the haor region. Farmers say embankments alone cannot protect their crops if rivers and canals cannot drain water efficiently.
The district has witnessed devastating flash floods in 1990, 1994, 2004, 2010, 2016, 2017 and 2022, when breaches in crop-protection embankments allowed upstream water to inundate vast areas of farmland. The losses ran into thousands of crores of taka, affecting hundreds of thousands of farmers.
The crisis has become more complex in recent years. In 2024, water levels in the haors and adjoining rivers remained almost the same, resulting in severe waterlogging that submerged immature Boro rice on around 80,000 hectares of farmland.
Farmers say the problem now occurs in two stages. During the dry season, sediment-filled riverbeds hold little water, creating an acute irrigation shortage. During the pre-monsoon period, the same rivers fail to drain water quickly, causing waterlogging that can destroy standing crops.
Sofor Uddin, 66, a farmer from Astama village in Joykalas Union of Shantiganj upazila, said farmers are increasingly trapped between late transplantation and early flooding.
“Water does not drain from the haor into the rivers on time, so transplantation starts about 15 days late. By then, irrigation water becomes scarce. Then even a little rain at the beginning of Baishakh can submerge the immature crop,” he said.
Abdur Rahman, a farmer from Dariyabaz village in Mollapara Union of Sunamganj Sadar upazila, said he cultivated six bighas of land with borrowed money last season, only to lose the entire crop to waterlogging after rainfall at the beginning of Baishakh.
“For a farmer, the loss of one crop can create a debt that takes years to repay,” he said.
According to Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), Sunamganj has 106 rivers and river channels across its 12 upazilas. Although most carry substantial volumes of water during the monsoon, around 70 become largely dry during the dry season.
The district's location near the Meghalaya hills of India further increases its vulnerability. Heavy rainfall in the upstream hills sends large volumes of water downstream within a short period, triggering flash floods. At the same time, sediment carried by the runoff gradually raises riverbeds, reducing their capacity to carry and drain water.
Bijon Sen Roy, former general secretary of Haor Bachao Andolon, said eight transboundary rivers—including the Chilai, Khasiyamara, Jadukata, Chela, Sonali Chela and Maula—along with more than 100 hill streams carry large volumes of water from Meghalaya into Sunamganj during the monsoon.
He said water from much of Sylhet also flows through the Surma and Kushiyara rivers before reaching the Meghna through the Dhanu River. Years of inadequate dredging have severely disrupted this interconnected drainage system.
“During the monsoon, the rivers are overflowing, but in the dry season many of them become almost completely dry. This indicates that the natural water-management system has been seriously damaged,” he said.
Retired professor Chittaranjan Talukdar, a former president of the Communist Party of Bangladesh's Sunamganj district unit, said river dredging has repeatedly been promised after major floods but has not been implemented on the required scale.
Md Obaidul Haque Milon, general secretary of the Sunamganj Haor and River Protection Movement, also called for immediate implementation of the dredging project.
“Authorities talk about river dredging whenever there is a disaster, but years pass without the project reaching the implementation stage,” he said.
The BWDB has proposed a major dredging project to address the problem.
BWDB Sunamganj Executive Engineer Mamun Hawlader said the proposal, titled ‘Improvement of Early Flood Management and Integrated Water Resources Management in the Haor Region,’ has been sent to the Ministry of Water Resources for approval.
The proposed Tk 1,429.84 crore project includes dredging 304 kilometres of 13 rivers, including the Surma, Kushiyara, Baulai, Dhanu, Ghura-utra, Upper Meghna, Old Surma, Chamti Darain, Abua, Patlai, Kaunai and Someshwari.
The proposed implementation period is 2026–2029, but the project has yet to receive approval.
“If approved, the project will improve water drainage, reduce waterlogging and help address irrigation shortages in the haor region,” Hawlader said.
Prabir Kumar Goswami, supervising engineer of the Water Development Board's North-Eastern Regional Office, said Sunamganj's location at the foot of the Meghalaya hills makes it naturally vulnerable to flash floods and water-management problems.
He said huge quantities of sediment are carried downstream every year by water flowing from the Indian hills, gradually raising the beds of rivers, canals and haors.
“Years of inadequate river dredging have made the problem increasingly severe,” he said.
With the next Boro season approaching, farmers fear that the unresolved dredging issue will once again expose them to the same cycle of delayed transplantation, irrigation shortages and waterlogging. They are urging the government to approve and implement the proposed project before another season of crop losses begins.

item.title: Three snakes found on 19th floor of secretariat
item.description:
Three snakes were found in the corridor of the Education Ministry on the 19th floor of Building No 6 at Bangladesh Secretariat on Thursday, raising questions about how they reached such a high floor.
Officials and employees first spotted two snakes in the corridor after arriving at work in the morning. Another snake was seen in the same area a short while later.
The offices of the education minister and education secretary are located on the same floor.
Officials who witnessed the incident said the snakes were seen moving through the corridor, causing panic among ministry officials and employees.
Ministry employees later killed all three snakes.
However, their species could not be immediately identified.
The ministry’s public relations officials confirmed the incident on Thursday afternoon and expressed surprise at finding three snakes together on the 19th floor of the Secretariat.
They said there could be more snakes inside a storeroom or elsewhere in the building, adding to concerns among officials and employees.
The incident has also raised questions about how the snakes managed to reach the 19th floor and whether there are other snakes inside the building.

item.title: Speaker: Disorder could threaten parliament’s functioning
item.description:
Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad Bir Bikram has warned that continued shouting, discourteous behavior and violations of parliamentary rules could seriously threaten Parliament’s functioning.
He made the remarks during the third session of the 13th National Parliament on Thursday following a commotion and exchange of words over statements by Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed and the opposition leader.
“The Rules of Procedure must be strictly followed to keep the democracy achieved through many sacrifices functioning and to make this institution of the people effective,” he said.
“The opposition has full freedom to point out the shortcomings and lapses of the government. But shouting in unison and silencing a minister without allowing him to finish his statement cannot be a healthy parliamentary practice.”
Recalling his nearly 40 years of parliamentary experience, the speaker referred to the bitter history of the past and urged lawmakers to learn from it and work toward building a better Parliament.
The opposition leader later resumed the discussion, referring to past instances in which statements were removed from parliamentary proceedings or sent for review.
He said the home minister’s remarks were clearly unparliamentary and alleged that similar incidents had occurred repeatedly.
He also questioned the speaker’s impartiality and protested the Speaker’s remarks that the treasury bench had more members.
The opposition leader said he did not support dividing Parliament based on numbers or status. He said the opposition would support the government on good initiatives and protest against wrongdoing.
He expressed hope that the speaker would conduct proceedings impartially and ensure equal dignity for all lawmakers.
Lawmaker Md Manirul Haque Chowdhury raised a point of order after part of his budget speech was removed from the proceedings for telling a metaphorical story.
He asked the speaker which word in his statement had been deemed unparliamentary.
Manirul also alleged that remarks about his beard and religious beliefs had undermined his personal dignity and the dignity of Parliament.
Seeking protection of his dignity, he asked the Speaker to respond formally to the notice and sought a resolution and ruling on the matter.
Responding to the overall situation, Hafiz Uddin said he had not been present when the incident involving Manirul occurred and would review the proceedings.
He said necessary action would be taken if anything unparliamentary was found.
“It is extremely regrettable that members are being prevented from speaking in the way they are,” he said.
The Speaker warned that Parliament could not function for long if lawmakers failed to follow his direction to sit down when asked.
Expressing disappointment over the disorder, he urged all sides to exercise patience.
The session was later adjourned for Asr prayers.
