Seedlings of BRRI Dhan-28, 29, 89 and 92, as well as Ranjit and various local varieties, were available. Eighty bundles were selling for Tk 350 to Tk 400. Seedlings of aromatic white- and black-grain varieties were considerably more expensive, with 80 bundles priced at Tk 700 to Tk 800.
Farmers said many of their own paddy seedlings had been damaged by prolonged dry weather, excessive heat, inadequate rainfall and irrigation shortages. As a result, they have been forced to depend on market-bought seedlings for Aman cultivation.
They also alleged that some traders and seedling producers were exploiting the increased demand to charge higher prices. According to farmers, the prices of paddy seedlings have risen nearly two to three times compared with last year.
Abdul Alim, a farmer from Padmapara village, said his seedbed dried up despite repeated irrigation efforts. “I could not save my seedlings despite providing irrigation and trying to protect them from the intense heat. I had no option but to come to the market, but the prices are too high,” he said.
Farmers Rafiqul Islam, Mozammel Haque and Bokul Pramanik of Thakurpara said rising diesel and irrigation costs had increased seedling production expenses. They added that paddy seedlings had also been damaged in some low-lying areas after fields were inundated.
Sonatala Upazila Agriculture Officer Krishibid Sohrab Hossain said the agriculture office was providing farmers with necessary technical advice to ensure successful Aman cultivation in line with the production target.
“Market monitoring is being strengthened to prevent paddy seedling shortages and ensure the sale of quality seedlings at reasonable prices,” he said.

item.title: Tk1,000cr spent, yet no end to Bhabodah waterlogging
item.description:
Despite more than Tk1,000 crore being spent on various projects over the past four decades, the Bhabodah region in Jessore is once again reeling from severe waterlogging, with more than a hundred villages submerged following days of continuous rain.
At Sujatpur village of Manirampur upazila, housewife Bithi Rani was desperately trying to save her family and belongings as rainwater entered her home. Recent rains had also submerged the fields, fish enclosures and roads, she said.
“There is waist-deep water in the yard, while the cowshed and kitchen are also flooded. We have moved our cattle to a higher road and are spending nights in a makeshift shelter there. Cooking has become extremely difficult. We are living with our children amid water, snakes and insects. How long will we have to live like this?” she asked.
Her suffering is shared by thousands of residents across Bhabodah. Continuous rainfall has inundated more than 100 villages in Manirampur, Keshabpur and Abhaynagar upazilas. Homes, schools, roads and religious institutions have gone underwater, forcing many families to take shelter on elevated roads with their livestock.
Locals estimate that around 80,000 people are currently waterlogged in several unions of the three upazilas. Thousands of fish enclosures have also been inundated. Shortages of safe drinking water, cattle feed and proper sanitation have made the situation increasingly difficult.
The latest crisis has raised fresh questions over the effectiveness of government initiatives. A Tk140 crore project launched in 2025 to dredge 81.5 kilometres of the Hori and Bhadra rivers had raised hopes of a lasting solution. However, recent rainfall has once again exposed the region’s vulnerability.
Residents blame the worsening situation on the failure to renovate the Amdanga Canal and inadequate drainage through sluice gates and rivers. They said a work order for the canal was issued two years ago, but work has yet to begin. The canal could potentially drain nearly 25% of Bhabodah’s water.
The river dredging project is also incomplete. Locals allege that a temporary embankment south of Kharnia Bridge and accumulated silt have obstructed water flow, worsening the waterlogging.
Iqbal Kabir Zahid, chief adviser to the Bhabodah Water Drainage Struggle Committee, said more than 200 villages across Jessore, Khulna and Satkhira had been inundated. He demanded immediate completion of the Amdanga Canal renovation, removal of temporary embankments and silt, phased implementation of Tidal River Management (TRM), and emergency food and healthcare support for affected people.
Jessore Water Development Board Executive Engineer Palash Kumar Banerjee said the obstruction near Kharnia Bridge had been removed and three sluice gates had been opened. More gates would be opened soon, he said, adding that water was draining rapidly.
Bhabodah covers parts of Abhaynagar, Manirampur and Keshabpur in Jessore and parts of Dumuria and Phultala in Khulna. Local activists say dredging alone cannot solve the crisis and that a coordinated, and long-term drainage plan is essential.

item.title: Three luxury cars seized in Cox’s Bazar over alleged import scam
item.description:
The Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID), Chittagong Regional Office, has seized three luxury cars in Cox’s Bazar over allegations that they were imported as parts and later assembled locally into complete vehicles.
The seized vehicles are a Toyota Supra, a Honda Civic and a Mazda MX-5.
Acting on a tip-off, a CIID team conducted a raid near the Ocean Paradise Hotel and Resort on Kolatoli Road in Cox’s Bazar on the night of August 27 and seized the three vehicles.
According to the CIID, the vehicles were allegedly brought into the country by declaring them as parts and were later assembled locally as complete cars.
During the operation, CIID officials also found that the vehicles were carrying markings reading “SINH4”, “S4FIAT” and “ESH4H” instead of conventional registration number plates.
The vehicles were seized under Section 191 of the Customs Act, 2023, pending verification of their import documents, ownership, customs declarations, payment of duties and taxes, and the legality of their local assembly, said a press release issued by the NBR.
The authorities suspect that the vehicles may have been imported by declaring different components as parts rather than as complete vehicles.
The investigation will determine whether the actual nature of the goods was concealed, false or incorrect declarations were made, or customs duties and taxes were evaded.
Section 33(2) of the Customs Act, 2023, may also be applicable if it is found that false information, statements or documents, or collusion, resulted in lower assessment of customs duties or charges or an erroneous refund.
If the investigation establishes that the vehicles were imported under the guise of other goods or through false or incorrect declarations, action will be taken under the relevant provisions of the Customs Act, 2023.
Five people have been identified as being linked to the vehicles: Hasibur Rahman Sinha of Cox’s Bazar, Azmain Raihan and Sharafat Rahman of Gazipur, and Nakibul Hasan and Sifiat Mahmud of Dhaka.
However, the investigation is still underway, and the authorities are verifying the ownership of the vehicles, their use, the individuals’ involvement in the import process and their roles.
Investigators will also determine how the different components entered Bangladesh and where and how they were subsequently assembled into complete vehicles.

item.title: ‘Ran for our lives:’ Tales of survival from Nepal-China disaster
item.description:
Some survivors of the deadly floods on the Nepal-China border ran for their lives, others narrowly missed disaster, but all were eyewitnesses to a major calamity and its aftermath.
Rescue crews in helicopters have been plucking survivors from along the valleys ravaged in the tsunami-like flow of water and debris apparently unleashed by a glacier’s collapse.
More than 1,400 people were still missing on Friday -- many of them foreign tourists -- and over 550 people were dead.
Here is what survivors told AFP:
Sivaranjani Muthunathan was travelling in Nepal by bus with 56 others from India’s southern state of Tamil Nadu. They were heading towards the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.
“Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told AFP, showing a video she recorded on her phone of a torrent surging towards her.
Vehicles were swept away or buried under mud around them.
“One by one, we also climbed out through the driver’s side,” she said, recounting how she had then scrambled up a hill.
Another pilgrim who was on the bus, 53-year-old Vijayabhuvaneshwari, said: “We had no choice.”
“Every vehicle in front of us, behind us, was gone,” she told AFP.
“As we were climbing up, we could hear what felt like explosions,” she said, giving only one name. “They were rocks and boulders crashing.”
With older members of the group struggling to climb the bank, Poonguzhali Ponmambadan, 61, unwrapped her sari dress and gave it to her husband to use as a rope.
“He used it as a harness to lift several old people,” she said.
More died than were rescued: Dam worker
Workers rescued from dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
“There were at least 400 workers at the site,” Dev Shrestha, who was airlifted from the site where he was working, told AFP after his rescue. “More people died than were rescued.”
Worker Buddha Tamang said he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck -- but he had managed to get out and reach help.
“I survived as I was in the tunnel,” said Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours.
“The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away.”
Another worker, Arjun Kumar Tamang, spoke of “massive damage” at the hydropower site where he had been.
“I don’t know how many people died but the force of the water swept everything away,” he said.
“I was at the powerhouse. I heard a loud noise. There was some seepage and we were told to come out,” said Ananay Sharma a 29-year-old engineer from India working on a project in the area.
“When I came out, everything was gone, only the river remained,” he added. “One residential camp completely washed away, another remains where we took shelter.”
Gorakh Khatka, an engineer who had been in the Shanti Bazar area near the epicenter of the disaster, ran for his life.
“All we got to react was 20 seconds before mud and water was as high as 20 feet (six meters) in the inundated area,” he said.
“We ran for our lives and spent more than 48 hours on a hill before help finally arrived.”

item.title: US judge rules Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic unlawful
item.description:
A United States federal judge has ruled in favor of the artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic in its dispute with the Pentagon over its labeling as a “supply chain risk.”
California district judge Rita Lin concluded that the label constituted an attempt by the government to make an example of Anthropic after the company refused to allow unrestricted military use of its technology and criticized the Department of Defense’s use of AI.
Lin wrote in a 59-page ruling that “the empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics.”
She said the government’s actions were “based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its ‘arrogance’ in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model.”
An Anthropic spokesperson said they welcomed the judge’s ruling, saying in a statement: “We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology.”
The dispute between the San Francisco-based firm and the government broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security after the company declined to allow unrestricted military use of its technology.
“We will not knowingly provide a product that puts America’s warfighters and civilians at risk,” wrote CEO Dario Amodei in a blog post back in February, adding that AI wasn’t reliable enough to be used in fully autonomous weapons systems and expressing concerns over mass surveillance.
In March, the Pentagon designated Anthropic a “supply chain risk” – a highly unusual label to apply to a US firm. The company complained of an “unlawful campaign of retaliation,” pointing out that the designation would have negative consequences for its business beyond defense deals.
Indeed, President Trump ordered all US government agencies to stop using Anthropic technology, calling it “a radical left, woke company” and “out-of-control” in a social media rant.
Defense Secretary Hegseth said companies would be expected to cut business links to Anthropic if they wanted to be considered for defense sector deals.
Shortly afterwards, OpenAI, Anthropic’s primary tech industry rival and operator of ChatGPT, made its own deal to work with the Pentagon.
In her ruling, Judge Lin, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, wrote that neither the US Constitution nor the federal statute the government invoked allows them to “impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic’s critique of the Administration’s views.”
Earlier in the legal proceedings, Lin had temporarily blocked the Pentagon from labeling the company as a supply chain risk and blocked enforcement of Trump’s social media directive ordering all federal agencies to stop using Anthropic and its chatbot Claude.
In a preliminary hearing on July 30, Lin had said that the government’s position was “really troubling” and seemed “at odds to me with the First Amendment.”
The White House is yet to comment on the decision.
In the coming weeks, Anthropic is expected to launch on the US stock market with an initial public offering (IPO) that could potentially eclipse SpaceX’s record Wall Street debut in June, which raised $86 billion.

item.title: King Harald, ‘symbol’ of Norway, dead at 89
item.description:
Norway’s King Harald has died aged 89, the palace said on Friday, his 53-year-old son Crown Prince Haakon automatically succeeding him on the throne.
Haakon takes over a monarchy long hailed for its modernity and modesty, but beset by a string of scandals in recent years.
“It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6:35am,” (0435 GMT) it said in a statement.
The flag at the royal palace in Oslo was lowered to half-mast, as crowds gathered outside the palace to pay their respects.
Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said he had received the news with “deep sorrow.”
“An entire nation mourns, and at the same time remains profoundly grateful for a long life devoted to Norway,” he said in a statement.
“King Harald loved Norway. And Norway loved its king.”
The government later announced a period of national mourning until the king was buried.
Hundreds of flowers had already been laid outside the palace the day before, after it announced the king was in “extremely serious” condition in hospital.
Vigdis Haug, 65, said she valued Harald’s ability to unify people.
“I think he has been such a down-to-earth king who has cared about all of us, and the words he always uses when he gives a speech are so wise and so valuable,” she told AFP.
Haug and others to whom AFP spoke pointed in particular to Harald’s speech after the neo-Nazi Anders Behring Breivik killed 77 people in twin attacks on July 22, 2011, in Norway’s worst massacre since World War II.
“He was someone who always seemed to find the words that brought us together and gave us a sense of security,” Caroline Vagle, a reporter for magazine Se og Hor, told AFP.
Neighboring Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf called him “an outstanding representative of his country. He gave ‘All for Norway,’” referring to Harald’s royal motto.
Denmark’s King Frederik meanwhile called the late monarch “an extraordinary man.”
Britain’s King Charles III said he mourned the death of his “dear cousin,” hailing Harald as a “towering figure.”
Harald was king when the Oslo Accords between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) were negotiated in the 1990s, and Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he was “deeply saddened” by his passing.
Church bells were to ring across Norway at noon (1000 GMT) to mark the king’s passing.
Haakon was to meet with the government on Friday to formally inform it of the monarch’s death, and to announce the royal name and motto he has chosen.
After that, the flag over the royal palace will be raised to the top again, while another flag on the royal balcony and at other official buildings will remain at half-mast until after Harald’s funeral.
Haakon’s 22-year-old daughter Ingrid Alexandra also automatically becomes crown princess.
Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, King Harald had been in hospital in Oslo since August 17, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991, embodied an open and tolerant Norway during his reign.
He faced mounting health problems in his final years, forcing him to scale back his official schedule.
But he always ruled out abdicating, arguing that he took a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament.
The past year has been a turbulent one for the Norwegian royal family.
In addition to his own health struggles, his wife Queen Sonja, also 89, was briefly admitted to hospital in May due to heart problems.
Haakon’s wife Mette-Marit is under scrutiny for her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Documents published in January in the United States revealed her sustained and at times intimate correspondence with Epstein between 2011 and 2014, at a time when the American financier had already been convicted.
In June, Mette-Marit’s son from a relationship prior to her marriage to Haakon, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes. He has appealed the verdict.
Suffering herself from a serious lung disease, Mette-Marit, 53, had to undergo a lung transplant in July.
The royals remain broadly popular with the Norwegian public, in large part to Harald’s unifying status and his unassuming, modest lifestyle.

item.title: KU admission tests set for Dec 17-18, KUET on Jan 8
item.description:
Khulna University (KU) will hold admission tests for first-year undergraduate (honors) courses for the 2026-27 academic year on December 17 and 18 next.
The decision was taken at a meeting of the university’s Central Admission Committee on Thursday, according to a notification signed by the university’s acting Registrar Prof Dr SM Mahbubur Rahman.
According to the notification, the admission tests for “C” and “D” units will be held on December 17.
The “C” unit covers disciplines under the Schools of Arts and Humanities, Social Sciences, Law, Education and Fine Arts.
The “D” unit includes disciplines under the School of Management and Business Administration.
The tests for “A” and “B” units will be held on December 18.
The “A” unit covers disciplines under the School of Science, Engineering and Technology, while the “B” unit includes disciplines under the School of Life Sciences.
Meanwhile, Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) will hold its first-year admission test for the 2026-27 academic year on January 8, 2027.
The test is for admission to BSc Engineering, BURP and B Arch programs.
To ease transportation and accommodation problems for students from different parts of the country, KUET has decided to hold the admission test at centers in three divisional cities – Khulna, Dhaka and Rajshahi.
The decision was taken following discussions on undergraduate admissions at the 118th special meeting of KUET’s Academic Council held on Thursday, university sources said.
The admission test will be held under the multiple-choice question (MCQ) system.
An admission test committee has already been formed to ensure the smooth conduct of the examination, the sources added.

item.title: Murgh Afghani: A creamy, smoky chicken recipe to try at home
item.description:
If you are tired of preparing chicken the same way every time, Murgh Afghani can bring a delicious change to your dinner table. The dish combines yogurt, cream, herbs, spices, and cashews with smoky grilled chicken.
Tahmina Zaman shared the recipe.
First, marinate the bone-in chicken with salt, lemon juice, ginger paste, garlic paste and chaat masala. Leave it for 15–20 minutes.
In a separate bowl, whisk together the yogurt, fresh cream, dried fenugreek leaves, black pepper, chaat masala and garam masala.
Blend the onion, coriander leaves, mint leaves, green chilies, and cashews into a smooth paste.
Add the yogurt mixture and the onion-herb paste to the chicken. Mix everything thoroughly and marinate the chicken for about one hour. If possible, marinate it for two–three hours for a deeper flavor.
Heat some ghee in a flat pan. Remove the chicken pieces from the marinade and pan-roast or grill them one by one.
Let the edges of the chicken char slightly. This smoky flavor is an important part of Murgh Afghani.
Heat a little butter and oil in a flat-bottomed pan. Add the remaining marinade and cook until the spices are well sautéed.
Add the grilled chicken pieces and a small amount of water. Cover and cook over low to medium heat for 12–15 minutes.
Once the gravy thickens and the oil begins to separate, turn off the heat and mix in about one tbsp of fresh cream.
For an extra smoky aroma, heat a small piece of charcoal with a clove and a little ghee in a small bowl.
Place the bowl in the middle of the chicken, cover the pan, and let the smoke infuse for about five minutes.
Remove the charcoal bowl and cover the chicken again for a few minutes.
Serve the Murgh Afghani hot with roti or naan.

item.title: Can too much chili powder harm your health
item.description:
Red chili powder is a common ingredient in South Asian cooking, adding color, flavor, and heat to curries, bhuna dishes, and other foods. Chili peppers contain capsaicin, the compound responsible for their spicy taste.
For most people, eating spicy food in moderate amounts is generally safe. However, consuming very large quantities of chili powder can cause discomfort and may worsen symptoms in people with certain digestive conditions.
Capsaicin can stimulate receptors in the digestive tract. In some people, particularly those who are not accustomed to spicy food, eating large amounts may cause stomach pain, burning, nausea or diarrhea.
People with sensitive stomachs may notice these symptoms more frequently.
Spicy foods may trigger or aggravate heartburn and acid reflux in some people. Those who already experience gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) may therefore need to limit foods that consistently cause symptoms.
If you regularly experience burning in the chest or upper abdomen after eating spicy food, reducing your intake and discussing persistent symptoms with a doctor may be appropriate.
A common belief is that eating chili powder directly causes stomach ulcers. However, current evidence does
Stomach ulcers are commonly associated with factors such as Helicobacter pylori infection and the frequent not support this claim. use of certain painkillers. Spicy foods may exacerbate symptoms for someone who already has an ulcer, but they are not considered a primary cause of ulcers.
People with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) or other digestive sensitivities may find that spicy foods trigger abdominal pain, bloating or diarrhea.
If you notice that symptoms repeatedly appear after eating heavily spiced meals, reducing the amount of chili may help identify whether it is a personal trigger.
Spicy foods are not generally considered a direct cause of asthma. However, very spicy foods can cause coughing, irritation or other unpleasant sensations in some people. Anyone with asthma who notices symptoms after eating particular foods should discuss the pattern with a healthcare professional rather than assuming chili itself is the cause.
The quality of chili powder also matters. Poorly stored spices can become contaminated with molds, while some products may be adulterated with unauthorized substances. Buying spices from reliable sources and storing them properly can reduce these risks.
Avoiding chili completely is not necessary for most people. Chili peppers contain capsaicin and other plant compounds, and research has explored their potential antioxidant and other health effects. However, many claimed benefits of chili—such as preventing cancer or causing major weight loss—are not established in humans.
There is no single amount of chili powder that is considered excessive for everyone. Tolerance varies from person to person.
A practical approach is to use chili according to your tolerance and reduce the amount if it consistently causes heartburn, stomach pain, diarrhea, or other discomfort.

item.title: The last piece of identity
item.description:
Mayyu Ali was born in 1991 in Maungdaw Township, Myanmar's Rakhine State (Arakan), the youngest of six children in a fisherman's family.
He writes under the name Mayyu, taken from the mountains and river near his childhood home. His early poems appeared in magazines in Myanmar. In 2017, he was among some 700,000 Rohingya who crossed into Bangladesh after the military operations that began on 25 August.
Two years later he had a poetry collection in print, an online platform of his own, and readers in camps holding close to a million people.
The literature he was joining had barely been written down. Rohingya is largely an oral language and, until recently, was rarely committed to paper.
It has also had little institutional footing.
A Rohingya-language program began on the Burma Broadcasting Service in August 1961; it was closed at the end of October 1965, on the same day as programs in Lahu and Pa-O.
The songs remain hard to find on paper. Documenting the tarana, a Rohingya song genre, the researchers Kazi Fahmida Farzana, Peter Sammonds, and Bayes Ahmed worked with Rohingya refugees in Malaysia.
They assembled their archive from the few lyrics that had been written down, from transcribing singers, and from recordings community members had made themselves.
Mayyu Ali. Photo: Collected
Their chapter appeared in Religious Sounds Beyond the Global North from Amsterdam University Press in 2024.
Before any of the anthologies, Ali printed The Blossom, a selection of his early poems, and distributed it around the camps.
In April 2019, two poets arrived from outside: the British poet James Byrne and the Bangladeshi-French poet Shehzar Doja.
Over two days they worked with twenty refugees in what they were told were the first creative writing workshops held in the camps. Ali had helped set them up.
He could not attend.
After the sessions, the editors asked participants to send work. The poems came in faster than they could be read—ten or more on some days. Few of the poets had pens or paper; almost all had mobile phones.
A planned pamphlet of about forty pages turned into a book.
I am a Rohingya: Poetry from the Camps and Beyond, published by Arc Publications in July 2019, ran to eighty-three pages: ten of the workshop poets, alongside Rohingya writers from the wider diaspora, poems in Burmese, three songs in Rohingya, and folk songs sung by Jani Alam. Many contributors used pseudonyms; being named would put them at risk.
The Poetry Book Society made it the inaugural title in its World Choice selection, chosen by the poet Ilya Kaminsky.
By then Ali had built something of his own.
In 2019 he and a group of friends launched Art Garden Rohingya, an online platform for Rohingya poetry and art—unfunded, with no institution behind it, run from inside the camps.
By 2022 it had gathered work by more than a hundred Rohingya poets, writers, and artists.
It has mattered particularly to women with few other routes into print. Shahida Win published her first poem there in 2019: "Thami Maha," Daughter the Great. She has said she wrote it after speaking with Rohingya women and girls about the discrimination they faced.
In 2020 she was selected by UNHCR as a youth leader and traveled to Geneva to speak on behalf of her community; in January 2023, she was invited to present her work at the Dhaka Lit Fest.
Others followed. The photographer Sahat Zia Hero founded Rohingyatographer in 2021, with support from the creative producer David Palazón.
The collective publishes a magazine and photobooks, among them Unseen Courage, curated in 2023 by Ishrat Bibi—the first monograph of work by ten Rohingya women photographers.
In 2024, it supported the historian Aman Ullah in publishing A History of Rohingyas to 1948. Separately, the Rohingya Cultural Memory Center in Cox's Bazar, an initiative of the International Organization for Migration, has identified at least twenty-three genres of Rohingya folk music, along with dozens of futhi—fairy tales told through song—and sixty-four sewing techniques.
Ali's own books span the years before and after resettlement.
Exodus: Between Genocide and Me appeared in 2019, while he was still in the camps; The White Elephant, an illustrated story told through the eyes of a Rohingya boy, followed.
He was resettled in Canada in 2021 and completed a master's degree at the University of Waterloo in 2024. His memoir, written with the French journalist Émilie Lopes, was published in French by Grasset in 2022 as L'effacement and in English in 2025 as Eradication, translated by Siba Barkataki.
The memoir makes one decision that repays attention: it does not begin with the burning. Reviewers note that it opens instead on the Purma River, on bamboo forests and morning mist over the Mayu Mountains, and on a boy learning the Burmese alphabet in classrooms shared with Rakhine and Hindu children. Belonging first, rupture afterwards.
He is not the only one writing from exile. Habiburahman, who reached Australia by boat in December 2009 and spent thirty-two months in detention before his release, remains stateless; he wrote First, They Erased Our Name with Sophie Ansel.
Ali now directs a Rohingya language preservation project at the Community Rebuilding Centre, transcribing oral traditions into Rohingya script with Burmese and English translations.
Four collections are complete. As the ninth anniversary of the exodus approaches on 25 August, the writing that might hold the language is being done in Ukhiya and Teknaf—and in the cities its authors have scattered to.
Ehatasham Ul Hoque Eiten teaches English at Daffodil International University, Dhaka, and writes on migration, identity, politics, literature, and education in South Asia.

item.title: In shadow of Premier League, Serie A flexes financial muscle
item.description:
For Italian football this has been a chastening year, yet, ahead of a likely frenzy before their transfer window shuts on September 1, Serie A clubs have spent the summer asserting their place in Europe's financial pecking order.
In both overall outlay and net spend, Serie A is a clear second among the 'Big Five' leagues.
While fee structures, conditional payments and financial sleights-of-hand can make the precise transfer values a little hazy, German site Transfermarkt on Thursday put Italy's total outgoings at more than one billion euros ($1.165bn), far ahead of La Liga, at three-quarters-of-a-billion, and then the Bundesliga.
In all, the 20 Serie A clubs are almost 430mn euros in the red this summer, against just under 300mn euros in Spain. Both the Bundesliga and French Ligue 1 are in profit.
Of course, the 'Big Five' is a misleading phrase. European club football has become the Premier League and everyone else. English clubs have, so far, spent 3.2bn euros, more than the other four league put together.
The second round of the Serie A season opens Friday with AC Milan, for now restored to their role as Italy's biggest spenders, hosting smartly-dressed yoyo club Venezia.
When Milan spent a reported 74mn euros to acquire Goncalo Ramos from Paris Saint-Germain, he became the most expensive Serie A signing since Juventus bought Dusan Vlahovic from Fiorentina five years earlier.
With Diego Moreira, coming from Strasbourg for 50mn euros, Milan have spent a total of almost 160mn euros, a whisker more than Juventus, with plenty of moves to come.
Under new boss Ruben Amorim, Milan opened the season with a 2-1 win at Torino.
On Thursday, Amorim did not rule out further recruits.
"We have to wait five more days until the transfer window closes," the Portuguese coach, who started last season in the Premier League with Manchester United, told his pre-match press conference.
"If someone arrives, it will be because they can help us both now and in the future."
He made clear that the transfer market was not simply about spending to bring players in.
"It's impossible to train during the week with 27 players. Nobody is going to be prepared, nobody is going to be satisfied, so there are some players that if they stay, they will not be part of the squad," he said, when asked about reports that the club was trying to unload Fikayo Tomori, Youssouf Fofana and Santiago Gimenez.
After a summer in which Italy missed the World Cup, sparking a debate on the lack of talent in the national team, Amorim said clubs need to develope from within.
"We need to take time and believe in our young players," he said. "We are going to have some problems with young players in some games, but big surprises happen.
"Everyone wants everything really fast and I'm a little bit old school. I think a lot of things will take time."
Yet on the opening weekend, five of the six biggest spenders, Milan, champions Inter Milan, Juventus, Roma and Napoli all won. The exception were Fiorentina, trying to spend their way into the top end of the table, who crashed to Roma.

item.title: Arteta braced for 'tough' Martinelli, Jesus exits from Arsenal
item.description:
Mikel Arteta revealed he has had difficult conversations with forwards Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus as both Brazilian internationals appear set to depart Arsenal.
"It's inevitable, at some point you need to have certain discussions and say certain things that sometimes are tough," said Arteta. Martinelli left training early on Thursday amid speculation he is set for a move to Saudi side Al Hilal for a fee that could reportedly rise to œ50million ($68 million).
"I think everybody knows and recognises how much we love Gabi (Martinelli). Whatever the outcome is, it will be because everybody agrees to that," added Arteta. Jesus has fallen well down the pecking order during an injury disrupted time in north London and was not even included in training on Thursday as he enters the final 12 months of his contract.
"It's something to do with the numbers that we have in the squad at the moment and the way we're managing that kind of situation individually with all the players -- they have some personal situations," Arteta said of the former Manchester City striker.
Arsenal have been linked with bolstering their forward line with a move for Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez. The Argentine is caught in an acrimonious stand-off after Atletico refused to let him depart the Spanish capital for Barcelona.
"Don't go there," said Arteta about Arsenal's interest in Alvarez. "I'm not going to make any comment about any player that is not with us." Ezri Konsa is already an Arsenal player and could make his debut back at Villa Park on Monday after securing a œ51 million move from Aston Villa.
The England international could receive a frosty reception but Arteta said that would not influence his decision in throwing Konsa into action.
"If I see something different in the player then I may have a question about that, but the way I've seen Ezri since day one, knowing his personality really well and through people that have worked with him, I have no concern there."
Bruno Guimaraes could also be fit to make his first competitive Arsenal appearance after missing the 3-0 win over Coventry last weekend due to a groin problem.

item.title: Welbeck scores first Chelsea goal in League Cup win over Luton
item.description:
Danny Welbeck netted his first Chelsea goal as the Blues shrugged aside third-tier Luton 2-0 at Stamford Bridge to reach the League Cup third round.
The front three of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers caught the eye in a 3-2 win at Fulham on Monday to open the Xabi Alonso era at Chelsea with victory.
But 35-year-old Welbeck showed he will be a useful addition to the Chelsea squad by heading in Malo Gusto's cross to break Luton's resistence after a goalless first half.
"I bring the average age a little bit higher!" Welbeck said on what he brings to a Chelsea squad that has lacked experience in recent seasons.
"The experience of playing games, being around loads of different dressing rooms and knowing what is a good dressing room and a bad one. Knowing what it takes to achieve something special."
Hakeem Odoffin's own goal killed the tie off after another dangerous delivery by Estevao as Chelsea set up a home tie against Leeds in the last 32.
Mike Penders started in goal for Chelsea after Robert Sanchez's error-strewn display against Fulham.
And Alonso may soon have the experience of Emi Martinez to count on with a deal to bring the Argentina international to London from Aston Villa reportedly close to completion.
But Martinez's international teammate Enzo Fernandez was not involved as he appears set for a move to Manchester City.
"We want to have a complete squad in all aspects. In quality, personality, young and experienced players -- so the young players get help, that they are still players to develop," said Alonso.
"I'm happy with the energy and attitude of the players."
Fulham also booked their place in round three with a 3-0 win over AFC Wimbledon.
First-half goals from Emile Smith Rowe and Rodrigo Muniz put Alvaro Arbeloa's side in command before Gonzalo Garcia came off the bench to net for the second time in two games since his move from Real Madrid.
Fulham travel to West Ham in round three.

item.title: Messi's Inter Miami appoint Gonzalez as new head coach
item.description:
Lionel Messi's Inter Miami on Thursday appointed his fellow Argentine Cristian "Kily" Gonzalez as new head coach of the reigning Major League Soccer champions.
Gonzalez, who hails from superstar Messi's hometown Rosario, will attempt to turn around Miami's poor run of post-World Cup form under interim manager Guillermo Hoyos.
"Inter Miami CF announced today that it has reached an agreement with Cristian Alberto 'Kily' Gonzalez to become the Club's new First Team head coach," said a club statement.
Hoyos will remain in post until his replacement's US work permit is approved, it added.
Gonzalez, 52, played left wing for European giants Inter Milan, Valencia and Zaragoza in a career that also included 56 international caps for Argentina between 1995-2005.
He moved into management in 2020, taking the helm at three Argentine club sides before his move to Miami.
The MLS Cup holders have endured a rough spell since the North American league's mid-season World Cup break, despite adding Brazil's Casemiro from Manchester United to a star-packed squad.
The side under Hoyos has lost four of its last five games, remaining second in the Eastern Conference but slipping 10 points adrift of leaders Nashville.
Hoyos on Thursday received a one-game ban and fine for the club's multiple violations of the league's late kick-off policy, his team repeatedly slow to return to the field after half-time breaks.
Hoyos, previously Miami's sporting director and a longtime friend of club captain and talisman Messi, only stepped into the temporary role in April after Javier Mascherano departed the club for "personal reasons."
"Inter Miami would like to especially highlight and thank Hoyos for his commitment and full dedication to the Club, demonstrated by his willingness to assume the role during this period, which began last April," said the club statement.

item.title: Raphinha, Lopez strike again as Barca beat Athletic
item.description:
Raphinha and Fermin Lopez goals helped Spanish champions Barcelona beat Athletic Bilbao 2-0 on Thursday in La Liga to continue their perfect start to the season.
The Catalan giants eased to a solid victory over their Basque visitors in their first game of the season at the partially-rebuilt Camp Nou, with new arrival Rodri coming on for his Barca debut.
Raphinha rounded the goalkeeper and slid home in the 37th minute to give Barca the lead, and Lopez netted after 82 minutes to secure the points, with the Catalans missing several chances for more goals and twice hitting the woodwork.
"Very happy to play my first game, happy with the victory, we've got two from two," Rodri told DAZN. "It's important to keep building up rhythm and adapting to this great team. My first minutes and (I had some) good feelings."
Barca coach Hansi Flick made three changes to the team that thrashed Elche 5-0 last weekend, handing Anthony Gordon his first start for the club, while bringing Pedri Gonzalez into midfield and picking Pau Cubarsi in defence.
The German kept Raphinha playing up front as a makeshift number nine, after the departures of Robert Lewandowski and Ferran Torres. Barca have fruitlessly tried to pry Julian Alvarez away from Atletico Madrid, who will not negotiate with the Spanish champions for the Argentina forward.
However, Raphinha netted twice from his striker's role against Elche and was on target again for Barca at Camp Nou, giving them a deserved lead at half-time. "It doesn't matter which position Rapha plays, as a captain he's shown total commitment to this team, to this club," Flick told reporters.
"You can see the supporters are connected with him and it's really good."
The Brazilian nodded against the post from Xavi Espart's cross midway through the first half and Lamine Yamal's follow-up effort was deflected wide, with Barca controlling the game. Eventually, they took the lead when Pedri slipped Raphinha through on goal, with the Brazilian rounding Unai Simon and rolling home.
Teenage star Yamal should have doubled Barca's lead before the interval but Simon made a fine save to deny him, while Gordon complained that he would have had an open goal if the Spain international had knocked the ball across to him. Gordon arrowed a shot narrowly over early in the second half as Barcelona probed for a second goal.
Yamal, still not at his best level since suffering a hamstring injury in April, hit the crossbar with an effort from the edge of the box. Simon saved twice from Lopez, who netted a brace in the opener. Flick sent on former Manchester City midfielder Rodri for his debut in midfield, leaving 10 Spaniards and Gordon on the pitch for Barca.
- Securing the points -
The champions were in the ascendency but Athletic threatened on a rare venture forward, with Oihan Sancet drilling against the post. Barcelona eventually found their second after a mistake from Athletic defender Aymeric Laporte, clumsily nudging Barca substitute Karim Adeyemi's cross past Simon, for Lopez to tuck into an empty net.
Adeyemi should have netted a third late on when Yamal picked him out at the back post but Simon denied the German from point-blank range. Yamal's second half performance was an improvement on a disappointing opening 45 minutes and his struggles against Elche, and Rodri said that the forward is improving.
"Maybe Lamine came from a moment where he was a bit down and today we tried to help him get back up and saw his best version, even though he didn't score," added Rodri, Spain's World Cup winning captain.
"The goals will come because the talent is there."
Athletic Bilbao have started their season with two defeats under new coach Edin Terzic. "I'm not a constant winner, I'm a constant trier," said former Borussia Dortmund coach Terzic.
"I'm fully of belief and trust when I see how we worked in these two games and in the training ground, sooner or later we'll get what we deserve and turn results in our favour."

item.title: Asha Bhosle's last film song set for September release
item.description:
The last film song recorded by singer Asha Bhosle, "Ae Meri Zindagi, Tu Chupi Hai Kahan," is scheduled for release on September 8, the makers of Om Ka Hari said.
Bhosle recorded the track in late 2023, when she was in her 90s. The film, directed by Harish Vyas, is a drama-comedy centered on a father-son relationship. Its cast includes Anshuman Jha, Raghubir Yadav, Soni Razdan, and Ayesha Kapur.
According to the makers, the release date was chosen deliberately, as it coincides with what would have been Bhosle's birthday.
Vyas said the timing was meant to honor the singer's body of work and its effect on listeners across generations.
Jha, who appears in the film, said the song holds a personal meaning for him, tied to the film's theme of a son expressing feelings toward his father that he never voiced in real life.
Bhosle died on April 12 this year at age 92. The cause was multi-organ failure, and she was being treated at Breach Candy Hospital in Mumbai at the time. Over a career of more than 70 years, she recorded upward of 12,000 songs and became known for tracks such as "Dum Maro Dum," "Piya Tu Ab To Aaja," "Chura Liya Hai Tumne Jo Dil Ko," and "Yeh Mera Dil."
A release date for the film itself has not been finalized.

item.title: Study of 4,500 animals reveals how human presence changes wildlife behaviour
item.description:
Wildlife may respond to the physical presence of people far more than scientists previously understood, according to a new study that tracked more than 4,500 animals across the United States.
Researchers from the University of California, Santa Barbara, the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, and Yale University combined GPS data from 37 animal species with anonymised cellphone location data.
The study, published in the journal Science, found that animals respond differently to human activity depending on the species and how much the surrounding landscape has already been altered by people.
The findings could help scientists develop more effective, species-specific approaches to wildlife conservation.
“Humans have complicated effects on wildlife — from our physical presence to how we reshape habitats,” said Ruth Oliver, an assistant professor at UCSB’s Bren School of Environmental Science & Management and co-lead author of the study.
The researchers took advantage of COVID-19 lockdowns, when restrictions sharply changed people’s movements. This created a rare opportunity to examine the effects of human presence separately from long-term changes to the environment.
The team studied weekly GPS records of 4,581 individual mammals and birds during comparable periods in 2019 and 2020.
To measure human movement, the researchers used anonymised cellphone location data with neighbourhood-level detail. According to the researchers, this was the first study to use such data to examine how people’s physical presence affects animal movement.
Scott Yanco, a research ecologist at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and another co-lead author, said the cellphone data provided a rare opportunity to measure the direct effects of human presence on wildlife.
The study found that 57% of the species examined were affected by both human presence and changes to the landscape. Human presence was associated with changes in the territory or environmental niche of 67% of mammal species and 68% of bird species.
About 67% of mammal species and 41% of bird species reduced the amount of habitat they used when faced with a combination of human presence and landscape changes.
Animals were particularly sensitive to people in areas with relatively little development, such as national parks, compared with heavily developed cities.
However, wildlife did not respond in the same way.
Wolves, for example, expanded their habitat use in response to human presence, possibly because they tend to move farther away from people or spread out to avoid human activity.
White-tailed deer showed a different pattern. Their environmental niche expanded as landscapes became more developed but became smaller as human presence increased. Sandhill cranes showed the opposite response.
Oliver said the findings highlight the importance of developing conservation measures for individual species because animals have different habitat needs, behaviours and threats.
The research is part of the COVID-19 Bio-Logging Initiative, an international project that examined how wildlife responded to the sharp drop in human activity during pandemic lockdowns, a period researchers described as the “anthropause”.
The wider initiative involved about 600 researchers and partners and collected around 1 billion location records from nearly 13,000 animals.
The researchers said combining animal GPS tracking with human movement data can help distinguish between the effects of infrastructure and the effects of people simply being present.
They are now investigating whether changes in animal behaviour caused by human activity and climate change help wildlife adapt or instead indicate stress that could increase their risk of death.
Oliver said the findings offer hope that better policies could help humans and wildlife coexist by identifying where and when animals need more space.

item.title: Five-year-old child killed in Rohingya camp gunfight
item.description:
A five-year-old child was killed in a gunfight between armed groups at the Kutupalong Rohingya camp in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, on Thursday evening.
The child, identified as Mojahed, sustained a gunshot wound to the head during the firing. His mother Tahera Begum and 6 others were also injured.
The gunfight took place around the B-40 and B-41 blocks of Camp-8 East at Kutupalong.
Police initially suspect that the gunfight took place between members of the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) and the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO).
Police Superintendent Asaduzzaman, deputy commander of the 8-Armed Police Battalion (APBn) assigned to Ukhiya, disclosed the incident on Friday morning.
Police and local sources said gunfire suddenly began in the camp on Thursday evening. More than 100 gunshots were heard, prompting many people to leave their homes and seek shelter.
Mojahed, son of Nur Alam, a resident of Camp-8 East, was rescued in critical condition and taken to Cox’s Bazar District Sadar Hospital. He died while undergoing treatment.
Among the seven injured, three were women, including Mojahed’s mother. Some of the injured were transferred from Cox’s Bazar Sadar Hospital to Chittagong Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.
A drive is underway to identify and arrest those involved in the incident.

item.title: Saudi fire victim returns home after eight years, buried in Rajshahi
item.description:
Shyamal Uddin Majhi, who was killed in a fire at a sofa manufacturing factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was buried beside his parents at his family graveyard in Bagmara, Rajshahi, at 11am on Friday.
His body reached his home in Dangapara village of Marugram under Jhikra Union of Bagmara upazila at around 3am on Friday.
The bodies of Shyamal and 9 other Bangladeshis arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight at around 4pm on Thursday. The bodies were then handed over to the relatives of the deceased.
Shyamal was a resident of Marugram under Jhikra Union of Bagmara upazila in Rajshahi district. His son-in-law Mizanur Rahman went to the airport to receive his body.
Mizanur said Shyamal’s namaz-e-janaza was held at 11am on Friday, with relatives and local residents attending. He was later buried beside his parents at the family graveyard.
Shyamal had gone to Saudi Arabia around 8 years ago in the hope of improving his family’s financial condition. He worked at a sofa manufacturing factory in the Manfuhah area of Riyadh.
On the night of August 9, a fire broke out at the factory, killing 16 Bangladeshi workers, including Shyamal.
Family members had been waiting for Shyamal to return home after 8 years. According to family sources, he had been preparing to return and had told them during their last conversation that he would return home soon.
His wife and 3 daughters had been waiting for him. His death has left the family facing uncertainty, as he was the family’s only earning member.
Local residents have called on the government, elected representatives, affluent individuals and those involved in expatriate welfare to stand beside the bereaved family.
Bagmara Upazila Nirbahi Officer Selim Ahmed said: “After hearing about the death, the upazila administration provided Tk 25,000 and dry food. They also received Tk 35,000 at the airport. Since the deceased has 3 daughters, I have asked prominent people in the area to look after them. As they are studying, we will support them.”
